news.title: Fired US General Leaked Iran, Russia War Details, Failed 3 Polygraph Tests
news.text: The Pentagon has accused a newly ousted three-star general of leaking sensitive information to the media just hours after officials confirmed his removal from a top military planning post.Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth fired Army Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia as head of strategy, plans and policy for the Joint Chiefs of Staff, a defense official said late Wednesday. Typically, the general in the position and their staff are responsible for generating and coordinating military plans for both the chairman of the Joint Chiefs and the president.No reason was given for the firing, the latest in a series of ousters or departures of military leaders under Hegseth. However, a Pentagon official, who was not authorised to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity, later said in a statement that Sylvia was under investigation over allegations of sharing classified information about the Iran war, the Russia-Ukraine conflict and other topics with journalists.The statement claims that Sylvia failed three polygraph tests about leaking classified information.Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a social media post that the department "took necessary personnel action to protect sensitive information" without mentioning Sylvia by name. He said the matter has been sent to the Justice Department for "potential further legal action."It is not clear why the Pentagon would appear to be pursuing charges in civilian courts instead of trying the general in the military justice system.Sylvia did not immediately respond to a voicemail, text messages, emails and a LinkedIn message on accounts and numbers that appear to belong to him.When asked about Sylvia's firing by reporters Thursday, President Donald Trump said, "She's gonna have big problems," incorrectly identifying the male general as a woman."We're very much looking for leakers," Trump said.In a confusing twist, the Joint Staff on Thursday also withdrew a statement from a day earlier that wished Sylvia well because "upon further review, we determined that the statement did not appropriately reflect the full circumstances."A spokesperson late Wednesday had said the Joint Staff extended its "deepest gratitude to Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia and his family for their 32 years of distinguished service to our nation."The firing of Sylvia from the Pentagon's top military planning post comes as Trump weighs renewed strikes on Iran in the eight-month-long war following next week's midterm elections. The Pentagon official, however, insisted Sylvia was not a "central planner" on the Iran conflict and said that was the purview of US Central Command.Before arriving at the Joint Staff, Sylvia served as commander of the 101st Airborne Division at Fort Campbell, Kentucky, until May 2025, according to his official biography, which has now been taken offline. He also previously served as the vice director for the office he recently led.His military awards include six Bronze Star Medals, including one for valor, and a Purple Heart, indicating he was wounded in combat.Sylvia's case is Hegseth's latest accusation against top Pentagon officials of leaking to the media. He fired three aides from his inner circle last year as part of a broader leak investigation that included polygraph tests.In a joint statement shared by senior aide Dan Caldwell, the trio protested the firing and said they were "incredibly disappointed by the manner in which our service at the Department of Defense ended. Unnamed Pentagon officials have slandered our character with baseless attacks on our way out the door."Hegseth never provided more information on what the three were accused of, and Caldwell would go on to be hired by the Office of the Director of National Intelligence.Under Hegseth, the Pentagon also has carried out a series of moves restricting media access, including requiring that journalists be escorted while on Pentagon grounds and declaring that its press office was a classified space inaccessible to journalists.(Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is published from a syndicated feed.)

news.title: Failed MAGA Mouthpiece Melts Down After Trainwreck Interview
news.text:
The press secretary Trump fired after five days is still fuming after her interview with Piers Morgan went off the rails. 

The former White House press secretary went after the Uncensored host, 61, on X on Thursday. A day earlier, their testy interview included Morgan telling her she “sounded like a robot.” 

On Wednesday’s show, Zacharia repeatedly refused to discuss her firing in an explosive back-and-forth. She said Morgan’s team had promised her the interview would include “a brief overview of my time as press secretary and then discussing the midterms.” 

Morgan told her on air that he had checked with his producers. “We haven’t misled you or misled anybody else,” he fired back.

Thursday’s X battle began when Zacharia replied to Truth Caviar, a pro-Trump X account run by Vadim Bichutskiy that bills itself as a MAGA “rapid response” operation. The account shared a clip of the interview, calling it “BRUTAL. JUST ABSOLUTELY BRUTAL.”

“I truly feel bad for @KatieZacharia,” the account wrote. “But does she understand how the news business works? How news gathering works? What is and isn’t newsworthy? Why even go on the show? Legitimate questions.”

Zacharia was quick to respond. 

“You can spin your bulls--t however you want,” Zacharia, 41, wrote in a reply link to X post to the Truth Caviar post 

“It was uncomfortable because Piers never got his Gotcha moment despite two attempts,” she wrote. 

Zacharia, 42, also accused Morgan’s team of “changing the topics” and of “not informing me Scaramucci was a guest.” Midway through their testy exchange, Morgan brought on Anthony Scaramucci, who held the record for the shortest stint in a top White House communications job until Zacharia came along. He lasted 11 days as Trump’s communications director in 2017.

“Others have a different take,” she added, sharing a screenshot of the California Post’s write-up of the interview using one of her quotes from the exchange: “I will keep fighting for him every single day. No matter how hard the media wants to spin, no matter how hard anchors, pundits, reporters, journalists want to spin what he is doing and focus it on me.”

Morgan, 61, hit back 21 minutes later.

“It got a lot less uncomfortable once Anthony joined us and you relaxed, stopped being a robot, and started answering questions like a human…” he wrote. “I wasn’t trying to ‘gotcha’ you, I was just asking you questions any journalist would ask you…”

Meanwhile, the Truth Caviar account also responded to Zacharia. 

“I support you, Katie, one post read. “You need to expect the unexpected when you go on shows like that.”

A follow-up added , “You were correct in not disclosing your private conversations with President Trump. That’s admirable, honorable, and loyal. But did you really think that your tenure as White House Press Secretary wasn’t going to be the main topic of discussion—regardless of what his producers told you?”

Zacharia had not yet responded at the time of publication. 

Meanwhile, she is leaning into the title she held for less than a week. Her X bio now reads: “Former White House Press Secretary for President Donald J. Trump | Wife & Mom of Four.”

But the new resume update is a far cry from the credentials that tanked her. Zacharia billed herself as a lawyer for years, a title Trump touted when he announced she would be the new press secretary. 

Her previous LinkedIn and bio listed a “General Counsel” role at a right-wing California nonprofit. But despite graduating from Pepperdine law school in 2011, she never passed the bar in any U.S. state. Her later claim that she’d passed the bar in China also fell apart. Foreigners aren’t allowed to sit China’s national bar exam or practice in its courtrooms. 

The Daily Beast has contacted Zacharia and Morgan for comment.

The former White House press secretary went after the Uncensored host, 61, on X on Thursday. A day earlier, their testy interview included Morgan telling her she “sounded like a robot.” 

On Wednesday’s show, Zacharia repeatedly refused to discuss her firing in an explosive back-and-forth. She said Morgan’s team had promised her the interview would include “a brief overview of my time as press secretary and then discussing the midterms.”

news.title: US General Fired By Hegseth Admits Leaking Classified Iran, Ukraine Info With Journalists: Report
news.text:
The Pentagon's top military planner, Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia, admitted to leaking classified information concerning Ukraine and Iran to two journalists from separate media outlets over a period of one year, according to an internal investigation report shared with Axios.
Sylvia was dismissed this week by US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth over the alleged misconduct. A US official told Axios that the career military officer acknowledged the leaks on video after failing four polygraph tests.
The investigation report accused Sylvia of making "unauthorised disclosures to the media". It also said he struggled to pass multiple polygraph examinations but cooperated with investigators by answering questions about his interactions with journalists and handing over his personal phone for forensic examination.
Leaks Allegedly Began In June 2025, Continued Through Signal
According to the report and US officials, Sylvia's alleged disclosures began as early as June 2025, before mainstream media outlets were removed from the Pentagon, and continued afterward.
The communications reportedly took place through the encrypted messaging application Signal. One meeting between Sylvia and a journalist also took place at a Silver Diner in Arlington, Virginia, after the reporter's access to the Pentagon was revoked.
"The meeting at the diner occurred because [redacted's] access to the Pentagon was revoked between meetings," the report stated.
During the meeting, Sylvia allegedly used notes he had taken while reviewing a classified report marked secret to orally share information about US assistance to Ukraine.
The report said the journalist was working on a book and had met Sylvia twice. It added that the general did not coordinate the meetings with the Pentagon's Public Affairs Office or seek approval to have the information reviewed before sharing it.
ALSO READ: Donald Trump Was Told Of Alleged Chinese Spy's Link To Nvidia Chief Jensen Huang Last Year: Report
Investigators Suspect Sylvia Deleted Signal Messages
The investigation also raised questions about the disappearance of communications between Sylvia and one of the journalists.
US officials suspect that the general deliberately deleted traces of their Signal exchanges but presented the deletion as accidental.
According to the report, Sylvia recalled receiving a Signal message from the journalist sometime in June or July, which he believed was related to Iran. He told investigators that he did not respond to the message and instead deleted it.
The report quoted him as saying that he believed he had accidentally deleted the entire message thread while removing the individual message. This also erased Signal messages and calls that would otherwise have been recorded on his personal phone.
In another instance, Sylvia reportedly acknowledged being one of the 20 officials cited in a media report that criticised Pentagon leadership.
Row Over Joint Staff Statement Supporting Sylvia
A separate dispute emerged over an alleged attempt by Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle's office to secure a statement from the Joint Staff supporting Sylvia following his dismissal.
A US official told Axios that Telle and his office had lobbied the Joint Staff to issue a statement backing the general in order to minimise the impact of potential future allegations that he had leaked classified information.
The Joint Staff reportedly withdrew the statement after someone within the Defence Department informed it of the reasons behind Sylvia's dismissal.
However, an Army official rejected the allegation that Telle's office had pushed for a supportive statement.
"This is the latest in a coordinated campaign of lies designed to sow chaos," the official said, adding that Acting Secretary Telle and his office had not advocated for any statement concerning Sylvia. The official described the entire account as false.
ALSO READ: Netanyahu’s Likud Loses Majority As Israel Election Count Ends, Arab Parties Gain Ground
Hegseth's Pentagon Steps Up Crackdown On Leaks
Sylvia's dismissal is the latest action in the Trump administration's broader effort to crack down on unauthorised disclosures and tighten restrictions on media access to the Pentagon.
In July, the Defence Department announced a joint task force with the Justice Department to identify individuals leaking information from the Pentagon. The department also called on its Office of General Counsel to prioritise prosecutions of those responsible for unauthorised disclosures to the media.
The Pentagon's approach to press access had already triggered a confrontation with news organisations. Last year, several defence reporters and media outlets surrendered their press credentials in response to restrictive reporting rules introduced by the department.
Sylvia did not immediately respond to a phone call, voicemail or text message sent to the number listed for him in public records, according to Axios.

news.title: Binance freezes $2.5 billion after suspected hack; Bitcoin sinks below $79,000
news.text:
A suspected hack of Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange, prompted it to freeze more than $2.5 billion in assets and sent the price of digital tokens tumbling. Binance said it hasn’t confirmed any impact to customer funds.

“We are aware of reports of a potential security issue and we are actively investigating,” a Binance spokesperson said. “At this stage, we have not confirmed any impact to user funds. Our security teams are reviewing all relevant information with urgency, and we will provide updates through official Binance channels as soon as we have verified information.”

Still, Binance said it has currently frozen $2.54 billion in assets and may raise that figure further as its teams work with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners.

Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao said the exchange may have been hacked but he expects all user funds will be fully covered. Zhao, who goes by CZ, no longer runs the company but remains its largest shareholder.

Online forums were rife with loss estimates and theories of how the attack was designed, none of them confirmed. Blockchain tracker Arkham has identified wallets associated with the suspected hacker holding about $5.9 billion in digital assets, though the figure does not necessarily represent the amount stolen from Binance.

Bitcoin slumped as much as 3.7% — falling below $79,000 to its lowest level since September — with other tokens also selling off. US stocks ended lower, with the Nasdaq 100 tech index dropping nearly 1.4%. 

“The rumored Binance hack is definitely driving down coin prices,” said Fredrick Collins, chief executive and co-founder of crypto data platform Velo Data. “Binance is such a behemoth in crypto that any hit to confidence in them is a hit to confidence in the industry as a whole, especially as people have already been skittish over the increasing cyber capabilities of AI.”

For crypto faithful who’d been basking in a two-month-long price rebound amid the tightening embrace of institutional Wall Street, the incident is a potential setback. Notorious episodes of theft and fraud among fallen crypto giants such as FTX and Mt. Gox set the stage for protracted bear markets in the past, bruises the industry has worked to put behind it in US President Donald Trump’s promised new era of regulatory clarity for cryptocurrencies.

To date, the biggest publicly known crypto hack occurred at exchange Bybit in February 2025, in which attackers made off with almost $1.5 billion of tokens. 

Binance said it has suspended withdrawals on multiple networks. “This is a precautionary measure and we are working to restore services as soon as it is safe to do so,” the company said in a statement.

An emergency insurance and reserve fund from Binance called the Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) was established in 2018 to serve a backstop for customers in “extreme situations,” according to the exchange. The SAFU fund is generally maintained at around $1 billion, but has fluctuated in the past in tandem with market movements, Binance said in 2024.

The two biggest stablecoin issuers said they took steps to freeze missing currency. Paolo Ardoino, the chief executive officer of Tether, said in an X post that it froze more than $1.5 billion of the stablecoin “related to a potential Binance exchange hack.” Jeremy Allaire, who runs Circle Internet Group Inc., said $800 million of its coin had been frozen amid “reports of a potential exploit involving Binance.”

“Hot wallets getting drained is not something new to crypto, but the amount would be a meaningful hack on the largest crypto exchange,” said James Seyffart at Bloomberg Intelligence. “It’s definitely a bad look. And this is one after another,” he said of a recent spate of security incidents.

Already fragile sentiment was hit further after a bruising run of crypto security incidents. In recent months, hundreds of millions of dollars were drained from Bitget, while tampering tied to Ledger devices also led to millions of dollars in losses. 

Traders had already been bracing for greater volatility in the crypto market this week, with $11 billion in options set to expire Friday. This comes days ahead of the US midterm elections taking place next week, when Democrats could potentially retake one or both chambers of Congress and open the door to greater regulatory scrutiny for the industry. 

Exchange thefts and malfeasance has been an ever-present backdrop of crypto’s almost two-decade ascent, the most famous of which was the collapse of Sam Bankman-Fried’s FTX in November 2022. In what remains perhaps the most notorious hacking incident, Japan-based Bitcoin exchange Mt. Gox was struck in 2011. Over time, the hackers made off with tokens worth billions of dollars based on the current market price. Mt. Gox eventually went bankrupt.

“It’s a huge damage to crypto because of the consistent successful hacks in the space,” said Tian Zeng, chief executive officer of crypto hedge fund Third Eye. “The fact that exploits keep happening makes it dangerous in the age of newest AI models being released every two weeks.”

The incident came on the same day event-contract venue Polymarket halted trading on its international exchange for an hour after it said that a third-party software provider was compromised. More than 700 Polymarket users were drained of $2.7 million in funds, said blockchain analytics platform Bubblemaps, in a post on X. A spokesman declined to comment on the numbers.

news.title: Ukraine Pauses Strikes on Russian Refineries Under US Pressure Ahead of Midterms – WSJ
news.text:
Ukraine has suspended strikes on Russian oil refineries following weeks of pressure from US President Donald Trump, as Washington seeks to contain rising fuel prices ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, according to a new report by The Wall Street Journal.

The unofficial pause began in mid-October and could continue beyond the US elections into November, the newspaper reported Thursday, Oct. 29, citing people familiar with Ukrainian military operations.

Ukrainian units conducting long-range strikes were instructed to suspend new missions against Russian refineries after completing operations already underway.

The decision came amid mounting tensions between Trump and President Volodymyr Zelensky, with Washington increasingly frustrated by Ukrainian attacks on Russia’s energy sector as diesel prices reached record highs.

The reported suspension has not been independently confirmed.

Trump sought a 30-day halt to refinery strikes

According to the WSJ, Trump’s adviser Jared Kushner pressed Ukrainian officials to halt refinery attacks for 30 days as a gesture of appreciation for Washington’s diplomatic efforts to negotiate an end to Russia’s war.

Kyiv sought assurances that Russia would reciprocate by suspending its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure or that Washington would provide additional Patriot air defense missiles.

Neither proposal produced a breakthrough, the report said.

European allies also encouraged Ukraine to exercise restraint, amid concerns about rising fuel costs and further deterioration in relations between Kyiv and the White House.

The pressure intensified after Trump publicly criticized Zelensky earlier this month, calling for Ukraine to replace its president and demanding an end to strikes on Russian oil facilities.

“He better damn well stop,” Trump said on Oct. 10, referring to Ukraine’s refinery attacks, according to an earlier WSJ report.

The remarks came as Trump announced an arrangement to increase purchases of Russian diesel and ease sanctions affecting Moscow.

The developments raised concerns in Kyiv that Washington was reducing economic pressure on Russia while demanding restraint from Ukraine.

Russia continues striking Ukrainian cities and energy facilities

The reported pause comes as Moscow continues its campaign of missile and drone strikes against Ukraine’s civilian and energy infrastructure, raising fears of widespread power and heating disruptions ahead of winter.

Russian forces launched another wave of attacks on Thursday, Oct. 29, killing civilians and damaging infrastructure across several Ukrainian cities.

In Dnipro, a Russian drone struck a crowded railway platform, killing at least 14 people. Additional attacks struck Chernihiv and Kremenchuk, while a late-night ballistic missile strike on Kyiv killed at least one person.

The continued bombardment highlights the absence of a reciprocal arrangement under which Russia would halt attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure in exchange for Kyiv suspending strikes on Russian refineries.

Ukraine has repeatedly defended its long-range drone campaign as a means of disrupting Russia’s war economy and responding to Moscow’s attacks on Ukrainian cities.

Ukraine’s domestically developed long-range drones have enabled strikes deep inside Russian territory, targeting refineries and other energy facilities far from the front lines.

The campaign has become an important tool for Kyiv to impose economic and logistical costs on Russia despite its smaller military and limited access to Western long-range weapons.

Ukraine’s dependence on US support complicates its position

The Journal reported that Ukraine’s reliance on American military assistance, intelligence-sharing and communications technology has made Kyiv vulnerable to pressure from Washington.

The deterioration in relations coincided with restrictions on Ukraine’s use of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet service, which temporarily disrupted some Ukrainian drone operations and air defense capabilities before service was restored.

Ukraine also depends on US-supplied Patriot air defense systems and interceptors to protect cities and critical infrastructure against Russian ballistic missiles.

According to the Journal, the dispute has further weakened Ukrainian confidence in Washington’s commitment to supporting Kyiv.

Midterm elections and US peace efforts

The timing of the reported suspension coincides with the final days before the Nov. 3 US midterm elections, when high fuel prices have become a sensitive domestic political issue for the Trump administration.

Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for rising diesel prices, although energy analysts point to the war in Iran and broader disruptions to global oil markets as the main drivers of the surge.

The Wall Street Journal reported that the suspension could last beyond the elections. 

The reported pause raises questions about why Ukraine is being pressed to halt strikes on Russian oil facilities while Moscow faces no comparable pressure to stop its relentless attacks on Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure.
news.summary: Ukraine reportedly suspended strikes on Russian oil refineries following pressure from President Donald Trump ahead of the Nov. 3 US midterm elections. According to The Wall Street Journal, the unofficial pause could extend into November, even as Russia continues attacking Ukrainian cities and energy facilities.

news.title: Trump at odds with reports of Vance’s letter to Iran
news.text:
President says outreach focused on medical supplies, not peace talks
• Tehran confirms receiving vice president’s letter, no response yet
• US media claims correspondence sought to avert new strikes

TEHRAN: Iranian media reported on Thursday that Tehran had received a letter from US Vice President JD Vance but had not yet responded, amid efforts to revive peace talks between the countries, though President Donald Trump said the outreach was about helping the country get medical supplies.

Iran’s semi-official Tasnim news agency reported that “Iran has received the letter, but has not yet responded,” while the Fars news agency carried a similar account, citing “a source familiar with the matter.”

The Wall Street Journal and The New York Times reported on Wednesday, citing US officials and people familiar with the matter, that Vance had sent the letter to Iranian Security Council chief Mohsen Rezaei at Trump’s direction in a bid to revive peace negotiations and avert new US strikes.

The letter and subsequent contact between US and Iranian officials focused on a possible framework for negotiations rather than specific terms for a peace deal, the Journal reported.

When asked by reporters later on Wednesday if he directed Vance to reach out to Iran to restart peace negotiations, Trump said, “No”.

“What that is is they need help with medical supplies and various things. He asked me what I thought. I said, if you want to do that, that’s OK. Basically, it’s getting supplies in to help people that are not well,” Trump told reporters.

Iran’s mission to the United Nations in New York and Vance’s office did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the letter and Trump’s remark.

The reported correspondence comes as diplomatic efforts to end the war have yet to produce a lasting agreement.

On Wednesday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran was discussing a plan with mediators, mainly Qatar and Pakistan, to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a waterway that normally carries about one-fifth of global oil consumption.

Qatari mediators presented Iran with a new draft deal Sunday to end the war, but a senior Iranian official said Doha had only put forward unacceptable ideas that did not amount to an offer.

Tehran insists that Washington meet seven conditions it has set for reopening the strait. The conditions include a ceasefire across the Middle East, the unfreezing of Iranian assets abroad, the lifting of sanctions on its oil sector and an end to the US naval blockade.

Tasnim reported that “any position that undermines this firm framework established by Iran is unacceptable”.

The war began Feb 28 with US-Israeli strikes on Iran that assassinated former Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and senior military commanders. Iran retaliated with attacks on Israel and US assets in the region, while the US imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports to starve it of oil export revenue.

Iran has long blamed US sanctions for hindering civilian access to medical supplies.

 Over 250 Colombians killed in Russia-Ukraine war, govt says 







BOGOTA, Columbia (AFP) — Over 250 Colombians have died and almost 1,000 have disappeared while fighting in the Russia-Ukraine war, the South American country’s foreign ministry reported Thursday.

Colombian nationals are sought in fighting around the world due to their extensive experience of armed combat, and thousands have been pulled into this conflict.

In Ukraine, 162 Colombians had died and 666 had disappeared, while on the Russian side, 94 had perished and 297 were missing, the ministry said.

Deputy migration minister Pedro Agustin Roa urged Colombians to “exercise extreme caution with job offers abroad, particularly those related to military activities.”

For “those who decide to leave the country to take part in international armed conflicts… there are limitations on consular protection and assistance in conflict zones,” he said.

Kyiv defends the legality of enlisting foreigners into its ranks while Moscow denies any links to recruitment networks to aid its invasion.

Families in Colombia have reported the mistreatment of their loved ones on the battlefield.

Trained for decades to confront powerful guerrilla groups and drug cartels in jungles and mountains, Colombian soldiers often struggle to find other forms of employment once they retire.

The United Nations estimates that at least 10,000 Colombian mercenaries are fighting abroad, lured by often false promises of high salaries and security and in many cases under inhumane conditions.

At least 7,000 of them have joined the Russia-Ukraine war, government data published in May showed.

news.title: US midterms: Trump skips rallies in two red states, takes phone route to rescue GOP
news.text: US President Donald Trump has cancelled his planned weekend rallies in Iowa and Kansas, opting instead to hold phone rallies to support Republican candidates in nearly 20 states ahead of the midterm elections.The move comes as Republicans face a tough fight to retain control of Congress, with several Senate races tightening in the final days of campaigning.Trump travelled to South Carolina on Thursday for the second time in a month to support Republican Senate candidate Darline Graham, who is facing a strong challenge from Democrat Annie Andrews. Republicans have not lost a Senate race in the state in nearly three decades, but growing voter frustration over the economy, high gas prices and the war in Iran has made the contest more competitive.The Republican National Committee (RNC) said Trump would instead lead a “72-hour sprint” of phone rallies, which could reach voters across nearly 20 states. The party said more states could be added to the schedule.Trump had earlier planned to hold rallies in Kansas on Saturday and Iowa on Sunday. He has held 25 rallies in October, short of his earlier target of more than 30.Asked whether health concerns had led to the cancellation, Trump dismissed the suggestion, saying, “I feel perfect.” He also said he did not need to visit Kansas, where Democrat Adam Hamilton is challenging Republican Senator Roger Marshall.Trump is scheduled to hold a rally in Daytona Beach, Florida, on Friday. It remains unclear whether he will hold more in-person events before election day.In South Carolina, Darline Graham was appointed in July by Republican Governor Henry McMaster to fill the Senate seat left vacant after the death of her brother, Senator Lindsey Graham. She later won the Republican nomination for a full six-year term.Trump praised her candidacy, saying, “She’s got the gene,” while attacking Democrat Andrews. Graham said Andrews would undo the work Republicans had done in Washington.Andrews, meanwhile, has urged voters to give her a chance, telling supporters that they could vote her out after six years if she failed to deliver.Republicans are also facing close contests in Texas, Ohio, Kansas, Iowa and Alaska, while both parties are closely watching the Mississippi Senate race.Democrats are hopeful of making gains, particularly in Ohio, where former senator Sherrod Brown is challenging Republican Senator Jon Husted. Brown has focused his campaign on rising living costs, accusing Husted of prioritising big businesses over ordinary families.In Alaska, Governor Mike Dunleavy has ordered an investigation after a New York Times report alleged that Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign was involved in recruiting a candidate with the same name as Republican Senator Dan Sullivan.The justice department has also issued new grand jury subpoenas as part of the investigation, according to a person familiar with the matter.Trump called the reported move a “conspiracy” and demanded that Peltola be removed from the ballot. Peltola dismissed the report as a distraction, saying the focus should remain on issues such as Sullivan's support for the war in Iran.With control of Congress at stake, both parties are stepping up their efforts in the final days of campaigning.You use AI every day. news.title: Pope Leo requested an absentee ballot in Illinois to vote in the midterms
news.text: Pope Leo XIV, a registered voter in Illinois, is poised to vote in next week’s midterm elections after he requested a mail ballot at his residence in Vatican City. Leo, whose birth name is Robert Francis Prevost, requested the ballot Oct. 3, the Will County Clerk’s Office chief of staff, Kim Fladhammer, confirmed to NBC News on Thursday. The Chicago Sun-Times first reported the ballot request. The clerk’s office told NBC News it has not yet received a completed ballot from the pope, who had lung cancer surgery this month. It is unclear whether he has filled out or mailed his ballot yet. If he does, it would be sent to Joliet, Illinois. And by virtue of becoming the first American pope in May 2025, Leo would be the first pope to vote in a U.S. election. Since he became pope, Leo has been an outspoken critic of certain Trump policies, including the U.S. war against Iran and the administration’s treatment of immigrants. Leo and President Donald Trump got into a back-and-forth in April after Leo called for peace in the war that began with U.S.-Israeli strikes on Feb. 28. Trump responded on social media by calling the pope “WEAK on crime” and “terrible for Foreign Policy” while taking credit for his papacy. “I’m not a big fan of Pope Leo,” Trump said at the time. Leo responded to the remarks, telling NBC News that he had “no fear of the Trump administration” and vowing to keep advocating for peace. Vice President JD Vance, who is Catholic, has also hurled criticism in Leo’s direction. Vance said he should “be careful” when he talks about theology, scolding him for his criticisms of U.S. foreign policy. Public records show that Leo has voted in previous elections, casting ballots in the 2012, 2014, 2018 and 2024 general elections. He also voted in Republican primaries in 2012, 2014 and 2016. Voters in Illinois do not register by party, and they can select which party’s primary they want to vote in each election cycle. Leo’s ballot this year includes a series of solidly blue races. His congressman is Rep. Jonathan Jackson, D-Ill., the son of the Rev. Jesse Jackson and the brother of former Rep. Jesse Jackson Jr., D-Ill., who is seeking re-election. Senate Democratic nominee Juliana Stratton, the state’s lieutenant governor, is seeking to succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Dick Durbin. Gov. JB Pritzker, meanwhile, is running for re-election, aspiring to become the first Democrat in the state elected to a third term as governor.
news.summary: It’s not clear whether Leo, who has been critical of the Trump administration, has mailed off his ballot yet.

news.title: White House Spews Vile Insults at Reporter After Trump Rage
news.text:
The White House is spewing vile insults at a reporter whom President Donald Trump lashed out at during a press gaggle Thursday. 

The “Rapid Response 47” X account, reportedly overseen by White House Communications Director Steven Cheung, has posted screenshots of Reuters White House reporter Jacob Bogage eating snacks in his car with the caption “sloppy!”

The screenshots were pulled from a TikTok of Bogage and his wife trying snacks on a road trip.

The disgusting attack came shortly after Trump exploded on Bogage for asking why he abruptly canceled a campaign rally with his must-win Senate candidate in Kansas. Bogage asked Trump, 80, if his decision had anything to do with fatigue from traveling so often for his cross-country midterm blitz. 

The sweat-soaked president did not take the question lightly. 

After asking where Bogage works, Trump fired back, “You are a SICK guy! Reuters is terrible, by the way. Look at this guy—he’s way out of shape... You are disgusting. Put yourself in shape. You look like hell.”

The White House took a victory lap over the surreal exchange between a president and a journalist covering the administration.

“@POTUS absolutely DESTROYS Fake News @jacobbogage,” the Rapid Response account wrote. 

Trump biographer Michael Wolff estimates that Cheung weighs about 400 pounds, making his apparent targeting of Bogage ironic. Wolff also alleged that Cheung has had collapsing fits associated with his size in the past.

“There’s a sort of tragic feel about (Cheung) because he’s so heavy,” Wolff said on the Inside Trump’s Head Podcast.

Cheung has made venomous attacks a hallmark of his White House tenure—particularly while targeting reporters who ask questions of the president and his declining health.

news.title: World's largest crypto exchange Binance freezes $2.54bn after suspected hack
news.text: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, said on Thursday that $2.54 billion worth of crypto assets had been frozen as it investigated a possible security breach. Stablecoin issuers Circle and Tether also froze assets linked to the incident, news agency Reuters reported."Binance will cover all hacking losses," Binance co-founder Yi He said.The exchange said the amount frozen could increase as it worked with law enforcement agencies, token issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and other industry partners to trace and freeze more assets.Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao, who no longer runs the company, said in a post on X that the incident "looked like a hack."Tether said it had frozen nearly $1.57 billion in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800 million.Binance said it was carrying out security checks and would resume withdrawals once the issue was fully resolved. It also assured users that their funds remained safe and said its teams were reviewing the incident. The exchange temporarily suspended trading on its Binance Alpha platform as a precaution.World Liberty Financial, a cryptocurrency company linked to US President Donald Trump and his family, said it had worked with crypto custodian BitGo to freeze funds stolen in what it described as a Binance hack.Yi He said $27 million in stablecoins and around $2 million worth of World Liberty tokens had been frozen.Crypto firm Ripple also froze around $200 million in funds, Yi said. Jack McDonald, senior vice president of stablecoins at Ripple, said the company was closely monitoring reports of a possible security breach involving Binance. He added that Ripple was freezing affected funds and coordinating with relevant parties.Miguel Morel, CEO of blockchain intelligence firm Arkham, said data suggested that billions of dollars may have been stolen from Binance by an unknown attacker. However, the exact cause of the incident had not been confirmed.Morel said the incident began around 4:30 pm EST and appeared to be ongoing.The incident adds to a series of cryptocurrency thefts. Attackers stole $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency in nearly 150 attacks last year, according to researchers at TRM Labs.In September, cryptocurrency exchange Bitget said around $350 million worth of crypto had been stolen from its platform, highlighting the security risks facing the industry.Authorities have warned that organised crime groups are increasingly using cryptocurrencies to move money across borders outside the traditional financial system.Binance allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets. It has more than 300 million registered users globally and around $160 billion in assets under custody, according to the exchange's 2024 annual report.Binance.US, a separate cryptocurrency exchange, said it was not affected by the security incident. Coinbase also said it was unaffected and was monitoring the situation.In a separate incident on Thursday, prediction market operator Polymarket temporarily halted trading following a security issue involving a third-party provider. news.title: Ex-Trump Aide Says Republicans 'Essentially in Triage' Ahead of Midterms
news.text: Former Trump administration official Marc Short has warned that Republicans are effectively in "triage" mode ahead of next week's midterm elections, as the party faces mounting challenges defending its majorities in Congress. Speaking on CNN Thursday, Short—who served as White House director of legislative affairs during President Donald Trump's first term and later as chief of staff to former Vice President Mike Pence—described the difficult political environment facing Republican candidates, with inflation, affordability concerns and allegations of corruption surrounding the White House threatening to undermine GOP enthusiasm. His assessment reflects concerns also voiced by senior Republicans. House Majority Whip Tom Emmer acknowledged earlier this month that the party was scaling back its electoral ambitions and becoming more selective about where it deployed campaign resources as the fight to retain its majority intensified. "It really is a business, and you're looking at a balance sheet, and you're putting your money where you're gonna get your biggest return," Emmer told Axios. "We expanded the map when we should have kept it narrow. We should have been conservative about what we were going after," he added. The comments come as Republican campaign groups increasingly shift from offense to defense, pulling back from some competitive races and redirecting millions of dollars toward protecting seats in traditionally Republican states, including Kansas, where incumbent Senator Roger Marshall faces a serious challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton. The Republican strategy increasingly resembles political damage control: prioritizing vulnerable candidates, pulling resources from races considered difficult to win and concentrating on limiting Democratic gains rather than expanding the party's majorities. Newsweek has reached out to the White House, Short and Pence for further comment. Marc Short Warns of Republican Enthusiasm Problem Short has argued that the Trump administration's economic record and allegations involving potential conflicts of interest are making it harder for Republicans to motivate voters. He warned that the challenges meant that Republicans are "essentially in triage"' ahead of Tuesday's midterm elections. "The White House policies, you know, they've not fixed the inflation challenge," Short said during another interview, on NewsNation, this week. He added that many voters felt their wages were not keeping pace with rising prices. He also pointed to what he described as an "avalanche of corruption stories" coming out of the White House, saying that the headlines were suppressing Republican enthusiasm. Short said that the climate was particularly damaging because Trump's original political appeal rested heavily on a promise to "drain the swamp" and challenge Washington's political establishment. "Yet that's where we now are," he said. Republicans Scramble to Defend Once-Safe Seats The difficulties described by Short are reflected in a broader Republican campaign strategy shift, with party groups increasingly prioritizing the defense of seats that were previously considered safe. Republicans have already pulled back from spending in the North Carolina U.S. Senate race, where Democratic former Governor Roy Cooper appears well-positioned to flip a Republican-held seat. GOP groups instead increased spending in South Carolina, where Republican Senator Darline Graham faces Democrat Annie Andrews in a surprisingly competitive contest. The same defensive strategy is playing out in Kansas, where Republicans are redirecting substantial resources to protect a seat that would ordinarily be considered safely within their reach. Despite Trump's 16-point victory in the state in 2024, Hamilton leads Marshall 49 percent to 45 percent in a CNN/SSRS poll. Republican groups have responded with millions of dollars in additional spending, including a $10 million commitment from the Senate Leadership Fund and advertising reservations totaling $1.6 million from a group linked to the Club for Growth. The investment illustrates how Republicans are being forced to defend traditionally safe territory as Democrats expand the electoral map. The defensive strategy extends beyond the Senate. In Nebraska's 2nd Congressional District, which includes Omaha, the Congressional Leadership Fund canceled $1.1 million in planned television advertising supporting Republican candidate Brinker Harding in the race to succeed retiring Representative Don Bacon. The move represented a significant reduction in national Republican support for the campaign, although other GOP groups remained active in the district. Meanwhile, Republican organizations redirected resources toward protecting seats elsewhere, including in Kentucky, Ohio and Texas. Democrats need a net gain of four Senate seats to take control of the upper chamber, while the House majority is also at stake. Republicans Turn to Attacks on Progressive Democrats Republican strategists are also attempting to shift the focus toward progressive Democratic figures, including Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (AOC) and Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. Short argued on NewsNation that highlighting progressive Democrats could help motivate Republican voters who are dissatisfied with their own candidates or unenthusiastic about the national political environment. "If you can't figure out a way to bring Republicans home right now because you're not excited about Ken Paxton, you might be excited to oppose AOC," he said, referring to the Texas attorney general's Senate campaign and the New York progressive. "You might be excited to oppose radical Democrats in the Senate. That may be actually playing more outside of Michigan than people appreciate," he added. news.summary: Ex-Trump administration official Marc Short says that Republicans are effectively in "triage" mode ahead of next week's midterms.

 Oraine Freestyle Adventures surpasses 30 million views, eyes global expansion 







If you have attended a major festival, concert or party in Jamaica or the diaspora, chances are you have spotted Oraine Freestyle Adventures capturing the excitement for his YouTube channel.

From high-energy dancehall performances to some of the most anticipated events on the entertainment calendar, the Jamaican-born content creator has built a digital platform that has amassed more than 30 million views and 91,000 subscribers since its inception in 2023.

For Oraine Dixon, the man behind the increasingly popular channel, the journey has been one of experimentation, persistence and a passion for Jamaican entertainment.

Operating out of New York City, Dixon covers major events across the Tri-State area, Jamaica and other destinations, with viewers in scores of countries: including England, Canada, Belgium, Mexico, Italy, Spain, Japan, Germany and several Caribbean territories.

Interestingly, the channel was not initially intended to focus on entertainment.

“When I started in 2023, it was actually a cooking channel. I wasn’t sure what I really wanted to do, hence the reason I gave it the name Oraine Freestyle Adventures. The numbers on the cooking videos weren’t what I was looking for, so I tried travel vlogs, but those weren’t connecting either. I then tried entertainment, and the rest is history,” Dixon said.

That transition proved to be a turning point, with his coverage of concerts, parties and festivals attracting growing attention.

Among the major Jamaican events he has documented are: Greatness Weekend, Best Weekend Ever and Vybz Kartel’s Freedom Street concert.

His international portfolio includes Vybz Kartel’s performances at Barclays Center in New York, Bounty Killer’s return to the same venue and Masicka’s Barclays Center concert.

Other events include Sunch NYC, Rise & Toast Brunch, Resurrection on the Green, Milk and Honey, and Daybreak.

For Dixon, the channel represents more than an opportunity to capture memorable moments. It is also a platform to promote Jamaica’s entertainment industry to international audiences.

“I love entertainment and I love Jamaica, so it brings me joy to share our culture with the world,” he said.

One of the most memorable moments in his journey came when dancehall veteran Bounty Killer offered him encouragement at a time when his channel had just 200 subscribers.

“Bounty Killer gave me my first endorsement when I was just at 200 subscribers. He gave me an intro and said, ‘Gwaan a road, youth!’” he recalled.

The gesture provided early encouragement as Dixon worked to establish himself in the competitive digital entertainment space.

Since then, he has witnessed firsthand how online content can influence travel decisions and contribute to entertainment tourism.

He pointed to his coverage of Best Weekend Ever, which he documented for three consecutive years, as an example.

“A lot of patrons who fly to Jamaica for that event would reach out to let me know they learnt about it by watching my channel. So right there and then, by them flying to Jamaica, that’s revenue for Jamaica,” he explained.

Originally from Old Harbour, St Catherine, Dixon attended Old Harbour High School and later lived in Spanish Town before migrating to the United States approximately 15 years ago.

Despite residing overseas, he remains committed to supporting the island’s entertainment industry.

“I live in the USA, but Jamaica will always be home. So anything to boost Jamaica, I will do it,” he added.

His growing popularity has also brought increased demand for his services, prompting him to consider expanding his operations.

“I don’t have any team members yet, but I’m considering building a team because for every booking I have, I get about three other people who need that same date, and it’s just me,” he shared.

Having already travelled to several states across the United States, Canada, Bermuda and Jamaica to document events, Dixon is now setting his sights on Europe.

He has received booking requests from England and other European destinations but has yet to pursue them, citing his apprehension about long-distance flights.

“My long term goal is to travel the world, as I’m already doing. I get bookings from England and Europe, but I haven’t gone yet. I need to build the courage to do long flights,” he said.

With an expanding subscriber base and growing international interest, Dixon is optimistic about taking Oraine Freestyle Adventures to new heights.

Left-wing late-night TV host Jimmy Kimmel suggested that former Alaska Governor Sarah Palin (R) is transgender while attacking President Donald Trump during Wednesday’s episode of ABC’s Jimmy Kimmel Live!.

Kimmel then moved on from Palin and returned to Trump’s original remark about child transgenderism, saying, “Does anyone actually believe this? If so, please trust me on this. If you drop off Timmy and he comes home Sarah, you picked up the wrong kid from school.”

This comment drew another loud reaction from audience members, who broke into applause.

“Turn the car around!” the left-wing host added.

 MoBay deputy mayor lauds Issa for 62-foot ‘Together We Rise’ monument 







ST JAMES, Jamaica — Deputy Mayor of Montego Bay Councillor Dwight “Debo” Crawford has hailed hotelier Christopher Issa for his role in transforming the city’s popular Jimmy Cliff Boulevard, describing a newly unveiled 62-foot monument commissioned by the businessman as a symbol of unity, resilience and renewed civic pride.

The towering sculpture, titled Together We Rise, by renowned Jamaican sculptor Scheed Cole, was unveiled Wednesday evening at 5 Jimmy Cliff Boulevard, popularly known as the Hip Strip, where Issa’s investments have helped reshape the tourism corridor.

“What we’re doing here tonight is far more than unveiling of a statue. This is the genesis of great thinking for the Hip Strip,” Crawford declared during the ceremony.

He described the artwork— two hands lifting a tree as people climb and build together— as representing the collective effort required to move Montego Bay forward.

“It tells our story. It’s about unity, resilience, and growth,” he said.

Crawford expressed confidence that the monument would inspire other businesses along the boulevard to invest in public art, culture and beautification.

He praised Issa, chief executive officer of S Hotel, for turning ideas into tangible developments.

“The S Hotel family and the stakeholders group have shown what happens when the private sector leads with heart,” Crawford said.

Issa explained that the idea for Together We Rise emerged from the success of another major installation commissioned by him and created by Cole — a 46-foot sculpture of Jamaica’s national bird, the streamer-tail hummingbird, popularly known as the doctor bird, mounted on the façade of S Hotel in August 2025.

The positive public response to the bird, encouraged him to consider another monument. The original plan was to celebrate Jamaica’s musical heritage, including mento, ska and reggae, but the devastation caused by Hurricane Melissa prompted a rethink.

“So the statue is not really about Melissa, but it was born of Melissa, and the message is, of course, the resilience of our Jamaican people, the suffering and loss of life that happened in really the strongest hurricane to this part of the world, and also the message of the help we got both from fellow Jamaicans and the international community,” Issa said.

He noted that the sculpture was completed in August, but the unveiling was held on the hurricane’s first anniversary to commemorate the disaster and the spirit of recovery.

Cole said the monument was also informed by his own childhood experiences of abandonment and the kindness of a woman who offered him food and shelter when he had nowhere else to turn. He credited that helping hand with influencing the course of his life.

“My life today is a consequence of a helping hand,” he said.

The sculptor explained that the lower section of the monument portrays survival amid rising floodwaters, with fingers depicting an elderly woman handing a baby to a younger relative in an effort to save the next generation, while a soldier reaches out to a distressed woman, urging her not to give up.

The upper section represents renewal, with images of people rebuilding and elements of Jamaican culture re-emerging. A tree rising through the structure symbolises life nurtured by shared love and support.

“If we do not walk hand in hand, then there is no future for us,” Cole said.

Janet Silvera, chair of the Hip Strip Stakeholders Group, also praised Issa, whose investments have helped change the face of Montego Bay.

“For me, he is Jamaica’s cultural icon, and he understands that,” Silvera said.

She said the monument is a valuable contribution to the city, adding to the cultural identity of a district that has experienced both vibrancy and decline.

The installation complements other initiatives commissioned by Issa, including colourful murals unveiled as part of an art walk created by S Hotel along Jimmy Cliff Boulevard, celebrating Jamaica’s musical heritage, particularly reggae, ska and dancehall.

news.text:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) told late-night host Jimmy Kimmel that he predicts the upcoming midterms will result in a “blue tsunami” that ends the Trump presidency “as we know it.”

Newsom appeared on Jimmy Kimmel Live! on Wednesday night to deliver his prognosis on the midterm elections.

“Donald Trump has a sell-by date in six days when his presidency ends as we know it,” said Newsom.

“This is going to be a blue tsunami,” Newsom added. “I’m not asserting something that’s not in evidence. You’re seeing all the early voting. It’s off the chart. The energy’s off the chart. People understand what’s at stake. It’s all on the line. Our founding fathers lived and died for this moment.”

Newsom added that the only open question will be whether or not Democrats take the U.S. Senate.

“It’s a legitimate open question about the Senate. But the House of Representatives is a fait accompli,” he added. “Finally, we’ll reinstate a co-equal branch of government, not a supine Congress like we know it today.”

When Kimmel expressed concern about how the administration will handle the midterm results, Newsom urged people to vote in droves.

“We see what he’s doing on a daily basis to literally suppress the vote, to set the conditions where he will then express doubt in the electoral outcome,” Newsom said. “The only way to defeat that is with margin. If we have a big enough margin in these races, he cannot contest those races.”

Newsom later revealed that he and the president’s relationship changed in the second term.

“In Trump 1.0, I probably talked to him every single week. The last call I had with him was almost 20 minutes, and it was just this stream of consciousness,” he said. “He was debating with me about not film tax credits, but how we should have tariffs for films around the globe. [He is] completely incurious. Not one question, no curiosity.”

“This is different,” Newsom concluded. “He’s not screwing around. There’s a ruthlessness of Donald Trump. So, again, with love and respect to my party, the Democratic Party, for things to change, we need to change. We’ve got to be more ruthless ourselves.”

news.text:
Washington, DC [US], October 30 (ANI): US President Donald Trump launched a personal attack on a journalist during a tense exchange with reporters on Thursday, body-shaming him over his appearance and telling him to "put yourself in shape" after being questioned about his health and decision to skip planned campaign rallies in Kansas and Iowa.

The exchange started when the reporter asked whether Trump's decision not to travel to Kansas was related to him feeling unwell after weeks of campaigning across the country.

Trump responded with sudden anger. "Oh, you're sick to ask that question. You are sick," he told the journalist.

When the reporter clarified that he was only checking on the President's well-being, Trump focused on the man's physical appearance. He briefly mimicked the journalist and repeated the question.

Also Read | Patrick Stewart Dies at 86: Legendary Actor of 'Star Trek' and 'X-Men' Fame Suffered From Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dementia.

"Look at this guy. He's way out of shape," Trump said.

Asked again whether he was feeling well, the President insisted he was in perfect health.

"I've been following me for two weeks. I feel perfect," he said, before launching a further personal attack.

"You are disgusting. Put yourself in shape. You look like hell," Trump remarked.

The confrontation followed Trump's decision to cancel planned weekend campaign appearances in Kansas and Iowa, where Republicans are facing competitive races ahead of Tuesday's midterm elections.

The rallies were scheduled for Salina, Kansas, on Saturday, and Dubuque, Iowa, on Sunday. Trump told reporters he did not "feel like I have to go to Kansas", whilst expressing confidence in Republican Senator Roger Marshall's prospects in the state.

The Republican National Committee later confirmed the cancellation of the Iowa rally as well.

Instead of appearing in person, Trump's campaign funding group, MAGA Inc., said it would organise a series of tele-rallies featuring the President in at least 19 states, including Kansas and Iowa, before Election Day.

Since October 1, Trump has held 25 rallies across 19 states as he campaigned to boost Republican candidates. The midterm elections will determine whether Republicans retain their narrow control of both the US Senate and House of Representatives.

Despite cancelling the two appearances, Trump is expected to travel to Florida on Friday for another campaign event.

The President has previously spoken about the physical demands of his campaign schedule. At a rally in Mississippi on Monday, he said, "God didn't make your vocal cords to do a rally every day." (ANI)

 ‘Star Trek’, ‘X-Men’ star Patrick Stewart dead at 86 







LOS ANGELES, United States (AFP)—Patrick Stewart, the British Shakespearean actor who became a Hollywood megastar through roles in the Star Trek and X-Men franchises, has died at the age of 86, an official statement said Thursday.

“We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife Sunny, following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia,” the statement said.

The actor, who hailed from the northern English region of Yorkshire, trod the boards in Britain with the Royal Shakespeare Company before crossing the Atlantic to enjoy an acclaimed career on the US stage and screen.

His best known Hollywood roles were as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation and Professor Charles Xavier in multiple X-Men and related Marvel films.

“His sonorous voice and singular talent will forever be synonymous with indelible performances in every genre,” the statement said.

“He explored the human condition in all its poetic complexity and brought hope not only to the far reaches of the Marvel Cinematic Universe, but into science fiction’s most iconic final frontier aboard the Starship Enterprise.”

news.title: Trump cancels Iowa, Kansas midterm events, opts for ‘tele-rallies’  - Bahamas Spectator – Bahamas &
news.text:
With only days left until the 2026 midterm elections, United States President Donald Trump has announced he will scale back his packed rally schedule, cancelling scheduled appearances in Iowa and Kansas.

The Republican National Committee (RNC) confirmed the cancellations in a statement on Thursday, unveiling a slate of “tele-rallies” to replace the cancelled events.

RNC Chairman Joe Gruters argued that the virtual appearances will be more efficient, reaching more voters than Trump otherwise could with on-the-ground stops.

“Voters across the country want to hear from President Trump before Election Day, and this 72-hour sprint will be a huge boost in the closing days,” Gruters said.

The tele-rallies will be broadcast to nearly 20 states, including battlegrounds like Michigan, Alaska, Texas and Iowa, where competitive races are unfolding for the US Senate.

The RNC statement added that further events may be announced in the coming days.

Trump’s rally on Friday in Daytona Beach, Florida – some 320 kilometres (200 miles) up the coast from his Mar-a-Lago resort – will proceed as planned.

Less than five days remain until the midterm elections on November 3, which will decide the composition of Congress, as well as key state and local offices.

Whichever party controls Congress will shape Trump’s legislative agenda during the final two years of his second term.

Trump has also expressed concern that the Democratic Party might push to impeach him for a third time if it wins majorities in both the House of Representatives and the Senate.

Currently, the Republican Party holds narrow majorities in both chambers. In the Senate, the party holds 53 seats out of 100. In the House, it has 218 seats, with all 435 offices up for grabs this election cycle.

The Senate, meanwhile, will see only about a third of its offices on the midterm ballot. Unlike in the House, where terms only last two years, senators are elected to six-year time spans, and their elections are staggered across different election years, to allow for greater stability.

Political forecasters have predicted Democrats have an advantage this midterm election cycle, citing Trump’s slumping poll numbers and voter blowback over cost-of-living issues, foreign policy and other concerns.

Harvard University’s ElectIt election forecasting model, for instance, has estimated that Democrats have a 94 percent chance of taking control of the House.

The race for the Senate, however, will be more difficult, with fewer seats available to win.

Trump has placed himself at the centre of the Republican strategy to defend the party’s congressional majorities. To motivate his base of support, he has repeatedly encouraged voters with the phrase, “Pretend I’m on the ballot.”

Midterm elections occur halfway through a president’s term, and they are often considered a reflection of a president’s popularity.

At 80 years old, however, Trump will be the oldest president by the time his term concludes, and his health has been a concern.

Since starting his second term, the Republican leader has been photographed with bruising on his hands, sparking speculation about any undisclosed medical conditions he may have.

After concluding a rally in South Carolina on Thursday, reporters inquired about his health.

“Mr President, you’ve been doing a lot of travel. We’ve been doing a lot of travel with you. How are you feeling? How’s your health?” a reporter from the news agency Reuters asked on the tarmac.

Trump, at first, dodged the question, focusing instead on his optimism about the Republican Party’s prospects in the election.

“We’re going to have a strong Tuesday night,” Trump said.

But the reporter continued with his line of questioning: “So you’re not going to Kansas has nothing to do with you being sick of travelling?” That prompted an irate reply from Trump, who lashed out.

“Oh, you’re sick to ask that question. You are sick,” Trump said, as he proceeded to insult the reporter’s weight.

“You’ve been following me for two weeks. I feel perfect. You are disgusting. Put yourself in shape. You look like hell.”

During his remarks to the reporter, Trump also questioned the need to visit Salina, Kansas, as he had planned to do on Saturday. “I don’t feel I have to go to Kansas,” the president said.

Kansas, normally a Republican stronghold, has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932.

But this election cycle, Republican Senator Roger Marshall is facing a tight race with Democrat Adam Hamilton, the pastor of a megachurch.

On Thursday, the news outlet CNN released a poll showing Hamilton up by four percentage points, leading with 49 percent support to Marshall’s 45 percent.

news.title: Pope Leo May Be Among the Nearly 20 Million Americans Voting Early
news.text: Pope Leo XIV requested a mail ballot for Illinois' November 3 midterm election, potentially putting the head of the Catholic Church on course to become the first pope known to cast a vote in a secular election while serving as pontiff. The Will County Clerk's Office disclosed that the pope, born Robert Francis Prevost, requested a vote-by-mail ballot on October 3. He remains a registered voter at a New Lenox, Illinois, address despite now leading the world's 1.4 billion Catholics from Vatican City. It's not known whether the ballot has been returned. "'Robert Francis Prevost is on the list of individuals who requested a vote by mail ballot for the upcoming election,'" Kim Fladhammer, chief of staff for the Will County Clerk's Office, told the Chicago Sun-Times. More than 20 million Americans and 1.16 million Illinois residents have voted early already. Any registered Illinois voter can vote by mail, including citizens living abroad under election law. Newsweek reached out to Will County election officials for comment. What Races Are on the Pope's Ballot? The pope's ballot is expected to include the Illinois U.S. Senate race to replace retiring Senator Dick Durbin, the reelection campaign of Illinois Governor JB Pritzker and various other Will County contests. Public records cited by the Sun-Times show Leo has voted in both Republican and Democratic primary elections in Illinois over the years, including Democratic primaries in 2008 and 2010 and Republican primaries in 2012, 2014 and 2016. Illinois does not require voters to register with a political party. He also voted in multiple general elections, including in 2024, according to the report. This would be his first major election since becoming pope last year. Tension Between the Pope and President Donald Trump Leo, the first American-born pope, has at times been at odds with President Donald Trump and some Republican officials over immigration policy and foreign affairs, particularly the war in Iran, although the Vatican has generally avoided direct involvement in U.S. electoral politics. In April, Trump criticized the pope as "weak on crime and terrible for foreign policy," with the pontiff responding that he had "no fear" of the Trump administration. Leo has strongly condemned the conflict in the Middle East and the "delusion of omnipotence" that caused it, saying this had led to "absurd and inhuman violence." What We Know About Pope Leo's Health The pope remembered to request a ballot just before he underwent surgery earlier this month to remove a portion of his lung, which was found to have cancer. Leo will not need further cancer treatment following surgery to remove a tumor from his right lung, the Vatican said, after final tests confirmed it was a localized lung adenocarcinoma. The pope's personal physician, Dr. Luigi Carbone, and his surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, said in a statement that results of the final post-operative tests on tissue removed during the surgery confirmed the initial diagnosis and that the cancer had not spread. "Today, the final histological examinations and molecular biology tests on the material removed during the Holy Father's surgery were reported. The results confirmed that the tumor was a localized lung adenocarcinoma. A subsequent oncological evaluation confirmed that no further treatment is necessary," the statement from the doctors read.
